usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger person
banmal, to a close friend or child
examples: A: 시험 100점 받았어요! / B: 와, 정말 잘했어요!
A: I got 100 on the exam! / B: Wow, you really did great!
the bare praise as an instant reaction to completed success
발표 끝나고 부장님이 후배한테 "수고했어, 잘했어" 하셨어요.
After the presentation, the manager told the junior, 'Good work — well done.'
a senior praising a junior: note the downward direction and banmal usage
애기가 혼자 신발 신었을 때 "우와, 잘했어! 최고야!" 하고 칭찬했어요.
When the toddler put on shoes alone I cheered, 'Wow, good job! You're the best!'
praising a child — 잘했어요 is a warm, completed-action praise, often stacked with 최고야 for encouragement
nuance: 잘했어요 is the everyday 'well done' that judges a COMPLETED action — built from 잘 'well' + 했다 (past of 하다 'to do'), so it always looks backward at what already happened. Crucially the praise flows DOWNWARD or sideways: a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, friends to each other — never upward. The decisive line is against 잘하시네요, which praises ongoing SKILL in the present ('you're good at this'), while 잘했어요 praises a finished result ('you did it well'). The English-speaker's chief pitfall is firing 잘했어요 at a boss or teacher — evaluating a superior's performance sounds presumptuous, as if you are grading them; to an elder, 수고하셨어요 (thank-you for the effort) is far safer than any praise of their work. Register: 잘했어 (banmal) ↔ 잘했어요 (polite) ↔ 잘하셨어요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 잘 + 했어요 literally means 'did well.' In practice it is a warm, downward-flowing compliment for a finished task — 'well done,' said after someone has completed something successfully. It always looks at the past.

Use it freely toward peers, children, or juniors after any completed effort — passing a test, finishing a task, making something. Never fire it upward at a boss or teacher; praising a superior's performance implies you are in a position to evaluate them, which feels presumptuous.

The decisive contrast is 잘하시네요 ('you're good at this') vs 잘했어요 ('you did well just now'): 잘하시네요 admires live, present skill, while 잘했어요 approves a finished result. Also: 수고했어요 thanks for effort without evaluating quality, while 잘했어요 evaluates the result.
Register ladder: 잘했어 (banmal, friends/children) → 잘했어요 (polite peers) → 잘하셨어요 (honorific). To deepen warmth: 정말 잘했어요, 진짜 잘했어. To a boss, skip evaluation entirely and say 수고하셨어요.

English speakers say 'well done' freely upward to anyone, including a supervisor. In Korean, 잘했어요 directed at a boss or teacher can feel condescending — you are grading their work. Even the honorific 잘하셨어요 is risky; the safer move toward a senior is gratitude (수고하셨어요), not evaluation.

mistakes: Saying 잘했어요 to your boss about their own work — evaluating a superior sounds condescending; thank them with 수고하셨어요 instead of grading them.
Confusing 잘했어요 (a finished action: 'you did well') with 잘하시네요 (a present skill: 'you're good') — using the wrong one means you praise the wrong thing.
Writing 잘 했어요 with a space — as a fixed praise expression it is written together, 잘했어요; the spaced 잘 했어요 reads as a literal description 'did it well'.

examples: A: (그림을 보여주며) / B: 와, 잘하시네요!
A: (showing a painting) / B: Wow, you're really talented!
the bare admiring reaction to a skill on display right now
요리 한 입 먹고 "어머, 요리 잘하시네요" 했어요.
After one bite I said, 'Oh my, you're a wonderful cook.'
complimenting a host's cooking mid-experience — the -시- signals upward respect
한국어로 인사하니까 직원분이 "한국말 진짜 잘하시네요" 하고 놀랐어요.
When I greeted in Korean the staff was surprised: 'Your Korean is really good.'
the go-to compliment Koreans give learners; respond modestly with 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요 — not 감사합니다 alone
nuance: 잘하시네요 is the present-tense 'you're good at this' said WHILE observing or experiencing someone's skill — 잘하다 'to be good at doing' + honorific -시- + the noticing ending -네요 ('oh, I notice'). Unlike 잘했어요, which judges a finished result, 잘하시네요 praises ABILITY in the moment. Because -시- and -네요 are baked in, it safely aims upward or sideways — toward an elder, a stranger, a host. The English-speaker pitfall is double: dropping the -시- (so 잘하네 alone to an elder is too casual), and treating the ubiquitous 한국말 잘하시네요 as a literal assessment of fluency — it is really a warm social icebreaker, and agreeing proudly with 네, 잘해요 sounds arrogant; the right reply is modest deflection such as 아니에요, 아직 멀었어요. Register: 잘하네 (banmal) ↔ 잘하네요 (polite) ↔ 잘하시네요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 잘하다 = 'to do well' + -시- (honorific) + -네요 ('I notice'). Literally 'I notice you do it well (respectfully).' In use, it is a present-tense admiration of live skill — 'you're really good at this' — aimed at what you are watching or tasting right now.

Say it while watching or experiencing a skill: a host's cooking, a colleague's calligraphy, a learner's pronunciation. With -시- it is safe toward elders and strangers. To a close friend, trim to 잘하네. The famous 한국말 잘하시네요 to a foreign speaker is social warmth, not a grammar report.

The dividing line from 잘했어요: 잘했어요 judges a past completed act ('you did well'), while 잘하시네요 notices present ability ('you're good at this'). Against 대단하시네요: 잘하시네요 credits a specific skill; 대단하시네요 expresses broad awe at a person's achievement or character.
Register: 잘하네 (banmal) → 잘하네요 (polite) → 잘하시네요 (honorific). Intensify with 진짜/정말: 진짜 잘하시네요. The variant -는데요 ending (잘하시는데요) adds a surprised, leaning-in admiration.

Two traps: (1) using 잘하네 to an elder (too casual — add -시-); (2) responding to 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud nod — Korean modesty convention expects 아니에요 or 아직 멀었어요; accepting the compliment openly reads as boastful.

mistakes: Answering 한국말 잘하시네요 with 네, 감사합니다 and a proud face — Korean modesty expects 아니에요 / 아직 멀었어요; agreeing sounds boastful.
Saying 잘하네 to someone older — the bare -네 is banmal; toward a senior you need the honorific 잘하시네요.
Using 잘했어요 when you mean present skill — 잘했어요 judges a finished act, while admiring live ability is 잘하시네요.

english: That's cool / You look great / How impressive.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
exclamatory -다, said to yourself out loud or as a sudden reaction
examples: A: (새 차를 보여주며) / B: 와, 멋있어요!
A: (showing a new car) / B: Wow, that's awesome!
the bare reaction to something stylish or impressive — can be about a thing or a deed
무대에서 춤추는 오빠 보고 "진짜 멋있다" 하고 탄성을 질렀어요.
Watching him dance on stage I exclaimed, 'That is so cool.'
everyday: 멋있다 praises style, vibe, or a cool deed — works for a performance or action
선배가 힘든 후배 도와주는 걸 보고 "선배님, 정말 멋있으세요" 했어요.
Seeing the senior help a struggling junior I said, 'You're truly admirable, sunbae.'
멋있다 praises admirable CHARACTER too, not just looks — and 으시- is required for a senior
nuance: 멋있어요 means 'cool / stylish / impressive' and stretches from a sharp outfit and a sleek car to an admirable ACTION or character ('that was a cool thing to do'). The critical split: 멋있다/멋지다 praise cool, dashing impressiveness — often applied to men or to anyone's bold deed — while 예쁘다 means pretty or cute (people, flowers, objects); calling a manly, athletic man 예뻐요 sounds off, while 멋있어요 fits perfectly. Near-twin 멋지다 carries a touch more exclamatory sweep ('how splendid!'), while 멋있다 is the casual everyday pick. The English-speaker pitfall is using 멋있다 as a filler 'cool' for everything — in Korean it carries genuine weight, so overusing it dilutes it; and many forget the honorific 멋있으세요 when admiring an elder's character or deed. Register: 멋있어 (banmal) ↔ 멋있어요 (polite) ↔ 멋있으세요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 멋 means 'style, flair, panache.' 멋있다 literally 'has flair' — in practice it covers looking cool, performing something impressively, or acting in an admirable way. It praises both the surface (style) and the substance (character).

Use it for cool looks, stylish objects, impressive performances, and admirable actions. Toward peers and younger people use 멋있어요; toward an elder who did something admirable, use the honorific 멋있으세요. Avoid it for cute or pretty things — reach for 예뻐요 or 귀여워요 there instead.

멋있다 vs 예쁘다: 멋있다 = cool/impressive/dashing; 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely/cute. A tuxedo and a brave act are 멋있다; a bouquet and a baby are 예뻐요. Near-twin 멋지다 sounds a touch grander and more exclamatory ('how splendid!'), while 멋있다 is the everyday casual pick.
Register: 멋있어 (banmal) → 멋있어요 (polite) → 멋있으세요 (honorific). Exclamatory: 진짜 멋있다 (said to oneself or as a burst). Boost: 완전 멋있어 (colloquial), 너무 멋있어요.

English 'cool' is a casual filler; Korean 멋있다 is a real compliment with weight, so sprinkling it indiscriminately dilutes it. Also: calling cute flowers or babies 멋있어요 is wrong (use 예뻐요), and forgetting the honorific 멋있으세요 when admiring an elder's admirable deed is impolite.

mistakes: Calling a flower or a baby 멋있어요 — that is 예뻐요; 멋있다 is for cool/impressive things and people, not cute ones.
Saying 멋있어 to an elder you respect — use the honorific 멋있으세요 when praising a senior's looks or character.
Spelling it 맛있어요 (delicious) by mistake — 멋 (style) vs 맛 (taste); one vowel flips 'cool' into 'tasty'.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
examples: A: (새 옷 입고) 어때요? / B: 우와, 너무 예뻐요!
A: (in new clothes) How does it look? / B: Wow, it's so pretty!
the bare compliment on someone's outfit or appearance
꽃다발 받고 "꽃이 너무 예쁘다" 하면서 좋아했어요.
Getting the bouquet I said happily, 'The flowers are so pretty.'
everyday: 예쁘다 covers objects — flowers, rooms, handwriting — not just people
아기 사진 보고 "어머, 정말 예뻐요" 했더니 엄마가 좋아했어요.
After seeing the baby photo I said, 'Oh, so adorable,' and the mom was delighted.
real situation: 예쁘다 for cute babies is a safe, warm compliment to a parent — much safer than complimenting a stranger's own face
nuance: 예뻐요 means 'pretty / lovely / adorable' and applies to people, clothes, flowers, babies, handwriting — anything visually pleasing or cute. The base 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular: drop 으 and add 어요 → 예뻐요 (never 예쁘어요). The three-way split learners miss: 예쁘다 = pretty/lovely, 귀엽다 = cutely endearing (puppies, a giggling toddler), 멋있다 = cool/impressive — a strong, handsome man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요, as the latter implies a more feminine, delicate beauty. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation (writing 예쁘어요) and aiming compliments at strangers: in Korean, commenting on a stranger's face unprompted can feel forward, so 예뻐요 lands most warmly on friends, children, and objects; complimenting an outfit is less invasive than a face. Register: 예뻐 (banmal) ↔ 예뻐요 (polite) ↔ 예쁘세요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 예쁘다 literally means 'pretty / beautiful (in a gentle, lovely way).' In use, it covers any visually pleasing thing: a person's face, a dress, a flower arrangement, neat handwriting. The prettiness it describes leans feminine and delicate rather than bold or impressive.

Freely used for objects, clothes, flowers, and children. For people, it is warmest between friends or toward younger people. Complimenting a stranger's face directly can feel forward; complimenting their outfit (그 옷 예뻐요) is less intrusive. For elders, soften with 예쁘세요.

Three-way split: 예쁘다 (pretty/lovely, people/things), 귀엽다 (cute/endearing, puppies, toddlers, something charming), 멋있다 (cool/impressive, bold actions, stylish men). A strong man is 멋있어요, not 예뻐요; a puppy is 귀여워요, not 예뻐요 — though 예쁘다 can stretch to puppies colloquially.
Irregular conjugation: 예쁘다 → 예뻐요 (not 예쁘어요), 예뻐, 예쁘세요. Intensify with 너무/진짜/정말: 너무 예뻐요, 진짜 예뻐. Exclamatory: 진짜 예쁘다 (said to yourself).

Two traps: (1) conjugating it 예쁘어요 — the 으-irregular drops 으, giving 예뻐요; (2) complimenting a stranger's face out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim 예뻐요 at friends, kids, or objects, or comment on an outfit rather than physical features.

mistakes: Conjugating it 예쁘어요 — 예쁘다 is a 으-irregular, so 으 drops before 어요: the correct form is 예뻐요.
Calling a cool, manly guy 예뻐요 — it implies pretty/feminine; use 멋있어요 for cool or handsome men.
Complimenting a stranger's face with 예뻐요 out of nowhere — it can feel forward; aim it at friends, kids, or objects, or compliment an outfit instead.

examples: A: 마라톤 완주했어요! / B: 와, 대단하세요!
A: I finished the marathon! / B: Wow, that's amazing!
the bare awe-reaction to an impressive achievement
혼자 아이 셋 키운다는 말에 "진짜 대단하세요" 하고 감탄했어요.
Hearing she raises three kids alone I said, 'You're truly remarkable.'
everyday: admiring someone's endurance or effort over a long period
사장님이 맨손으로 회사를 일으킨 얘기를 듣고 "정말 대단하십니다" 했어요.
Hearing the CEO built the company from nothing I said, 'That is truly remarkable, sir.'
real situation: the formal -십니다 form for a respected senior; 대단하다 fits whole-life achievements
nuance: 대단하세요 expresses genuine AWE at someone's achievement, effort, or character — 대단하다 'to be remarkable' + honorific -세요. It is heartfelt admiration for something impressively hard ('I could never do that'), which is why its default form already points upward with -세요. The dividing line from 잘하시네요 is scale: 잘하시네요 praises a specific SKILL ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses being overwhelmed by the WHOLE accomplishment or person ('that's incredible'). The English-speaker pitfall is the bare 대단해 toward an elder — natural between friends, but to a senior it sounds flippant; use 대단하세요 or formal 대단하십니다. A subtler trap: 대단하다 can flip to sarcasm with a flat tone ('oh, wonderful...'), so deliver it with clear warmth. Register: 대단해 (banmal) ↔ 대단해요 (polite) ↔ 대단하세요 / 대단하십니다 (honorific/formal).

structuredNuance.t: 대단하다 literally means 'to be great/remarkable' (not from a 한자 compound most learners recognize). In use, it conveys genuine awe — 'I'm blown away by what you did or who you are.' The honorific -세요 is the default because the expression naturally points at someone admirable.

Use it for genuinely impressive feats — raising three children alone, building a company from scratch, finishing a marathon at 70. It aims naturally upward or sideways. Toward an elder or boss use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다. The banmal 대단해 is warm between friends but sounds flippant to a senior.

대단하세요 vs 잘하시네요: 잘하시네요 praises a skill ('you're good at this'), while 대단하세요 expresses awe at a whole accomplishment ('incredible'). Against 존경스러워요 ('I respect/admire you'): 존경스럽다 is more formal reverence toward a person's overall stature; 대단하다 reacts to a specific feat.
Register: 대단해 (banmal) → 대단해요 (polite) → 대단하세요 (honorific) → 대단하십니다 (formal). Noticing variant: 대단하시네요. Intensified: 정말/진짜 대단하세요.

Two traps: (1) saying bare 대단해 to an elder — use 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다; (2) delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, how wonderful...'), so lean into warm delivery. Also: reserve it for genuinely impressive things; using it for minor tasks (nice soup!) dilutes it.

mistakes: Saying 대단해 to an elder or boss — the bare banmal can sound flippant; admire a senior with 대단하세요 or 대단하십니다.
Using 대단하세요 for a minor everyday compliment — it carries real awe, so reserve it for genuinely impressive feats, not 'nice shoes'.
Delivering it flatly — 대단하다 can read as sarcasm ('oh, wonderful'); say it with clear warmth so it lands as praise.

english: Go for it! / You can do it! / Good luck!
usage: go for it / you got this
the officially correct Korean spelling, same word and meaning
rallying a group together before a shared challenge
examples: A: 나 이제 면접 보러 가! / B: 화이팅!
A: I'm off to my interview! / B: Go get 'em!
the bare one-word cheer just before a challenge — often with a raised fist gesture
시험 앞둔 친구한테 "내일 시험 화이팅!" 하고 메시지 보냈어요.
I texted my friend, 'Good luck on tomorrow's exam!'
everyday: the standard pre-exam text; you can add 너 할 수 있어 for extra encouragement
마라톤 나가는 선배께 "선배님, 화이팅 하세요!" 하고 응원했어요.
Since my senior was running a marathon I cheered, 'Go for it, sunbae!'
real situation: add 하세요 to make the cheer politely address someone older — bare 화이팅 alone to a much older person is too light
nuance: 화이팅 (borrowed from English 'fighting') is Korea's universal pre-effort cheer — 'go for it, you've got this, I believe in you' — shouted before exams, interviews, games, or any challenge, often with a raised fist. By itself it is casual and friendly; toward someone you respect, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. The dividing line is against 힘내세요: 화이팅 pumps up ENERGY before an effort that has not started yet ('push!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone who is already in the middle of a struggle ('hang in there'). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: never read it as 'let's fight' — it was borrowed purely as encouragement; and the bare 화이팅 in a formal or very hierarchical setting feels too light, so use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다. Spelling note: 파이팅 is the officially standardized form, but 화이팅 is what most Koreans actually write.

structuredNuance.t: 화이팅 looks like the English word 'fighting' but it was borrowed purely as an encouragement cheer — 'go for it / push hard / I believe in you.' There is no aggression implied. Think of it as Korea's 'allez' or 'vamos': pure forward energy.

Ideal before any challenge: an exam, a job interview, a first day at work, a sports match, a presentation. Between friends and peers, bare 화이팅 is perfect. To a senior or in a formal setting, attach a verb: 화이팅 하세요. There is no honorific form of the cheer-noun itself — politeness rides on the attached verb.

화이팅 vs 힘내세요: 화이팅 fires before the effort starts ('go!'), while 힘내세요 comforts someone already struggling ('hang in there'). Against 잘될 거예요: that reassures about the outcome ('it'll be fine'), while 화이팅 charges up the person's energy.

Both spellings are accepted: 화이팅 (common casual writing) and 파이팅 (official standard). Polite form: 화이팅 하세요. Group cheer: 우리 화이팅! Combo: 화이팅, 잘할 수 있어! Written online as 핫팅 or 팅 (very informal shorthand).

Two traps: (1) reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight' or 'I'll fight you' — it is borrowed encouragement, not aggression; (2) shouting bare 화이팅 at a much older person or in a formal setting — it feels too light; use 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다 instead.

mistakes: Reading 화이팅 as 'let's fight / I'll fight you' — it is borrowed to mean encouragement ('go for it'), never literal fighting.
Shouting bare 화이팅 at a senior in a formal setting — soften it to 화이팅 하세요 or 잘하시길 바랍니다.
Assuming 파이팅 is wrong — it is actually the standardized spelling; both are accepted, with 화이팅 more common in casual writing.

english: Cheer up / Stay strong / Hang in there.
usage: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
formal -십시오, in a serious or public setting
stay strong, it'll all be okay
pairs comfort with reassurance — a common complete phrase
examples: A: 요즘 너무 힘들어요 / B: 힘내세요. 다 잘될 거예요.
A: Things are so hard lately / B: Stay strong. It'll all work out.
the bare encouragement + reassurance combo for someone struggling
시험에 떨어진 친구에게 "너무 속상해하지 마, 힘내" 했어요.
To my friend who failed I said, 'Don't be too upset — hang in there.'
everyday: comforting a friend after a setback, in banmal; 속상해하지 마 softens the blow first
상을 당한 동료에게 "많이 힘드시죠. 힘내세요" 하고 위로했어요.
To a grieving colleague I said, 'This must be so hard. Stay strong,' as comfort.
real situation: acknowledge the pain first (힘드시죠) before saying 힘내세요, especially in serious loss
nuance: 힘내세요 literally means 'bring out your strength' (힘 'strength' + 내다 'to bring out' + -세요) and is the warm 'cheer up / hang in there / stay strong' said to someone who is tired, sad, or going through hardship — encouragement for an ONGOING struggle, which is the key dividing line from 화이팅 (a pre-event pump-up for something about to start) and 잘될 거예요 (reassurance about the outcome). The English-speaker's register pitfall is bare 힘내 to an elder or struggling senior — use 힘내세요 toward anyone you are not very close with. The cultural trap is using 힘내세요 as the lead phrase at a funeral or in heavy grief: it can feel like pressure to 'snap out of it', so for serious loss Koreans first say 얼마나 힘드세요 (acknowledging the pain) or 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다 before any encouragement. Register: 힘내 (banmal) ↔ 힘내세요 (polite) ↔ 힘내십시오 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 힘 'strength' + 내다 'to bring out / exert' + -세요. Literally 'please bring out your strength.' In practice it is the warm, empathetic 'hang in there / stay strong / you can get through this' — comfort directed at someone already in difficulty.

Use it when someone is tired, failing, grieving, or overwhelmed — ongoing hardship, not a challenge about to start. 힘내 is warm banmal for friends; 힘내세요 is polite for colleagues, acquaintances, or elders in moderate difficulty. For very serious grief (bereavement), first acknowledge the pain before saying 힘내세요.

화이팅 vs 힘내세요: 화이팅 cheers on an effort about to begin; 힘내세요 comforts someone already in struggle. 잘될 거예요 vs 힘내세요: 잘될 거예요 reassures about the outcome; 힘내세요 strengthens for the present moment. They stack naturally: 힘내세요, 다 잘될 거예요.
Register: 힘내 (banmal) → 힘내세요 (polite) → 힘내십시오 (formal). Warmth boost: 진짜 힘내세요, 꼭 힘내세요. Common pair: 힘내요, 다 잘될 거예요.

Two traps: (1) using bare 힘내 toward an elder or boss (too casual — 힘내세요 is safer); (2) leading with 힘내세요 at a funeral or in profound grief — it can sound like pressure to 'cheer up'; acknowledge the pain first with 얼마나 힘드세요 or 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.

mistakes: Saying bare 힘내 to an elder, boss, or grieving senior — use 힘내세요; the banmal can sound dismissive of their hardship.
Using 힘내세요 as the main thing said at a funeral — it can pressure the bereaved; lead with 얼마나 힘드세요 or 삼가 고인의 명복을 빕니다.
Confusing it with 화이팅 — 힘내세요 comforts someone already struggling, while 화이팅 cheers on an effort that hasn't started yet.

english: Good work / Thanks for your effort.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or junior after finishing
good job / thanks for the work
banmal, to a close friend or junior
thank you for your hard work
formal honorific, to a senior or in business
you went through a lot / well done
warmer variant that stresses the toil and empathizes with difficulty
examples: A: 일 다 끝냈어요! / B: 수고했어요.
A: I finished all the work! / B: Good work.
the bare acknowledgement when someone wraps up a task
퇴근하면서 동료에게 "오늘도 수고했어요" 하고 인사했어요.
Leaving work I said to a colleague, 'Good work again today.'
everyday: the standard end-of-day workplace farewell — almost formulaic at Korean offices
발표 잘 마친 후배한테 "준비하느라 고생 많았어, 수고했어" 했어요.
To the junior who finished their presentation I said, 'You worked hard preparing — well done.'
real situation: acknowledging both effort (고생) and completion (수고했어) feels fuller and warmer
nuance: 수고했어요 (수고 'effort/trouble' + 했어요) thanks and acknowledges someone for the EFFORT they put in — said after a task wraps up, at the end of a shift, or as the routine workplace 'good work' when everyone goes home. The critical rule is DIRECTION: it normally flows to peers or DOWN to juniors. Saying it to a clear superior is contested — many Koreans feel a junior shouldn't 'grade' a boss's labor, so toward a senior, 감사합니다 or 오늘도 고생하셨습니다 is safer. The dividing line from 고생했어요 is tone: 고생했어요 emphasizes the toil and difficulty ('you really went through a lot') and feels more empathetic, while 수고했어요 is the neutral standard acknowledgement. Register: 수고했어 (banmal) ↔ 수고했어요 (polite) ↔ 수고하셨습니다 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 수고 means 'trouble, effort exerted for someone else.' 수고했어요 literally 'you went through effort' — in practice it acknowledges and thanks someone for completing work: 'good work / thanks for your effort.' It is retrospective, always said after the task is done.

Say it at the end of a task, shift, meeting, or day. It flows DOWNWARD (senior to junior) or SIDEWAYS (peers). Toward a boss or elder, it can feel presumptuous — as if you are grading their work. Use 감사합니다 or 오늘도 고생하셨습니다 upward. At Korean workplaces, 수고했어요 between departing colleagues is nearly obligatory.

수고했어요 (neutral effort-acknowledgement) vs 고생했어요 (warm, empathetic — stresses the hardship: 'you really went through a lot'). 수고하세요 (to someone still working, farewell: 'keep up the good work') vs 수고했어요 (to someone who finished, past tense).
Register: 수고했어 (banmal) → 수고했어요 (polite) → 수고하셨습니다 (formal). Farewell to someone still working: 수고하세요. Combined warm version: 고생 많으셨어요. Emphatic: 정말 수고 많으셨습니다.

Two traps: (1) saying 수고했어요 to your boss — it implies you are evaluating their labor, which a junior does not do; thank them with 감사합니다 instead; (2) mixing up 수고했어요 (finished, past) with 수고하세요 (still working, farewell) — the tense difference matters completely.

mistakes: Saying 수고했어요 to your boss or a clear senior — it can read as a junior grading their effort; use 감사합니다 or 고생 많으셨습니다 carefully instead.
Using bare 수고했어 with a senior — drop to 수고하셨습니다; the banmal upward is rude.
Treating 수고하세요 (to someone still working / leaving) and 수고했어요 (to someone who finished) as the same — present 하세요 vs past 했어요 changes the meaning.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
축하드리다 — swap 하다 for 드리다 toward elders or bosses
examples: A: 저 합격했어요! / B: 와, 진심으로 축하해요!
A: I passed! / B: Wow, congratulations from the heart!
the bare congratulation as an instant reaction — 진심으로 adds sincerity
친구 결혼한다고 해서 "결혼 진심으로 축하해" 하고 꽉 안아줬어요.
My friend said she's getting married so I hugged her tight and said, 'Congratulations on your wedding, truly.'
everyday: name the occasion first, then 축하해 — the natural word order
부장님 승진 소식에 "승진 진심으로 축하드립니다" 하고 인사드렸어요.
On the manager's promotion I said, 'Congratulations on your promotion, sir.'
real situation: toward a senior, 축하드립니다 (humble -드리다) is the respectful choice, not plain 축하해요
nuance: 축하해요 (祝賀, 축하 'congratulation' + 해요) is the all-purpose 'congratulations' for any happy milestone — passing, a wedding, a promotion, a baby, a birthday. The key politeness move is the humble verb: to an elder, boss, or in formal settings, swap 하다 for 드리다 → 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다, which humbly 'offers' the congratulation rather than plain 해요. The dividing line is 축하해요 (neutral polite, peers) vs 축하드립니다 (humble formal, upward). The English-speaker pitfall is word order and particles: the natural Korean pattern is OCCASION FIRST — 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요 — with no object particle needed in speech; learners often put 축하해요 first, or add 을/를, both sounding unnatural. Register: 축하해 (banmal) ↔ 축하해요 (polite) ↔ 축하드립니다 (humble/formal).

structuredNuance.t: 축하 (祝賀) is Sino-Korean for 'congratulation' (祝 = pray/wish, 賀 = celebrate). 축하해요 = 'I congratulate you.' In use, it is the standard celebratory phrase for any positive milestone — passing, marriage, promotion, or birth.

Freely used at any happy milestone. To peers and juniors, 축하해요 or bare 축하해 is natural. To an elder, boss, or in formal settings, use the humble 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다 — the 드리다 form 'offers up' the congratulation and shows deference. Bare 축하해 to a senior is too casual.

축하해요 (neutral polite, any occasion) vs 축하드립니다 (humble, upward formal). Against 잘됐어요 ('that's great news'): 잘됐어요 is a warm reaction to good news but not a formal congratulation; 축하해요 is the proper celebratory phrase.
Register: 축하해 (banmal) → 축하해요 (polite) → 축하드려요 (humble polite) → 축하드립니다 (formal). Warmer: 진심으로 축하해요, 정말 축하드려요. Written card: 축하합니다.

Word order trap: in Korean the occasion comes FIRST — 합격 축하해요, 생일 축하해요. Learners say 축하해요 합격 (backwards) or add object particles (합격을 축하해요), which sounds textbook-stiff in casual speech. Also, never use plain 축하해요 for a boss — the humble 축하드려요 is required.

mistakes: Saying 축하해요 to a boss or elder — use the humble 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다; plain 해요 is for peers and juniors.
Word order like 축하해요 생일 — the occasion comes first: 생일 축하해요, 합격 축하해요.
Adding an object particle (합격을 축하해요 in casual speech) — in everyday talk it is just 합격 축하해요, no 을/를 needed.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
생신 = honorific noun for an elder's birthday + 드리다 for respectful offering
격식 -합니다, a written card or formal ceremony
examples: A: 저 오늘 생일이에요! / B: 어머, 진짜요? 생일 축하해요! 오늘 뭐 해요?
A: Today's my birthday! / B: Oh really? Happy birthday! What are you doing today?
the natural A/B reaction when someone announces their birthday — 진짜요 shows warm surprise, then the wish lands immediately
친구한테 "생일 축하해! 선물 따로 샀어" 하고 건넸어요.
I said to my friend, 'Happy birthday! I bought you a separate present,' and handed it over.
everyday: the casual banmal greeting between friends, often texted or said at a party
할머니께 "할머니, 생신 축하드려요. 오래오래 건강하세요" 하고 인사드렸어요.
To my grandmother I said, 'Happy birthday, grandma. Please stay healthy for a long, long time.'
real situation: 생신 (honorific noun) + 축하드려요 (humble verb) — both upgrades are required for a grandparent
nuance: 생일 축하해요 is 'happy birthday' — 생일 'birthday' + 축하해요 'congratulations.' The single most important upgrade for learners: an ELDER's birthday uses the honorific noun 생신, not 생일, so for grandparents or a respected senior you must say 생신 축하드려요 / 생신 축하드립니다; using plain 생일 for a grandparent sounds under-polite. The dividing line is exactly 생일 (peers/juniors) vs 생신 (elders), paired with 해요 vs 드려요. The English-speaker pitfall is attempting to calque 'happy' with 행복한 or 즐거운 — Korean does NOT say 행복한 생일; the structure is built on 축하 'congratulate', making it literally 'I congratulate you on your birthday.' Register: 생일 축하해 (banmal) ↔ 생일 축하해요 (polite) ↔ 생신 축하드립니다 (honorific/formal).

structuredNuance.t: 생일 = 'birthday'; 축하해요 = 'congratulations.' So 생일 축하해요 literally means 'I congratulate you on your birthday,' not 'happy birthday' in the English structural sense. The English calque 'happy birthday' (행복한 생일) does not exist in Korean — the phrase is built on congratulating, not wishing happiness.

Use 생일 축하해요 for peers and younger people. For grandparents, parents, or any respected elder, BOTH the noun and verb must upgrade: 생신 축하드려요 / 생신 축하드립니다. Using plain 생일 for a grandparent's birthday is a noticeable under-politeness. Warm additions: 건강하세요, 행복하세요, 오래 사세요.

생일 (neutral) vs 생신 (honorific noun for elder's birthday) — the noun itself changes for elders, unlike most Korean politeness which only changes verb endings. 생일 축하해요 vs 생일 축하합니다: -합니다 is for written cards, speeches, or ceremonies; -해요 is for spoken everyday use.
Register: 생일 축하해 (banmal) → 생일 축하해요 (polite) → 생신 축하드려요 (humble polite to elders) → 생신 축하드립니다 (formal). The birthday song uses -합니다: 생일 축하합니다.

Two traps: (1) calquing 'happy' as 행복한 생일 or 즐거운 생일 — Korean says 생일 축하해요, built on 축하, not 'happy'; (2) saying 생일 축하드려요 to a grandparent but keeping the plain noun 생일 — the noun must be 생신 for elders, not just the verb.

mistakes: Saying 생일 축하해요 to a grandparent or elder — their birthday is 생신, so it should be 생신 축하드려요 / 축하드립니다.
Calquing 'happy' as 행복한 생일 or 즐거운 생일 — Korean uses 축하 'congratulate': it is 생일 축하해요.
Writing 생일축하해요 with no space — 생일 and 축하해요 are separate words and should be spaced.

english: It'll work out / Things will be fine.
usage: polite -요, reassuring a peer or younger
다 'all' makes the comfort broader and warmer
examples: A: 합격할 수 있을까요? / B: 물론이죠, 잘될 거예요.
A: Do you think I'll pass? / B: Of course — it'll work out.
the bare reassurance about an uncertain outcome — 물론이죠 adds confidence
걱정하는 친구한테 "너무 걱정 마, 다 잘될 거야" 했어요.
To my worried friend I said, 'Don't worry too much, everything will work out.'
everyday: pairs naturally with 너무 걱정 마 — one phrase addresses the worry, the other addresses the outcome
수술을 앞두신 분께 "분명히 잘되실 거예요. 제가 응원할게요" 하고 위로했어요.
To someone facing surgery I said, 'It will surely go well. I'm rooting for you.'
real situation: honorific 잘되실 거예요 for a senior + 응원할게요 for deeper comfort
nuance: 잘될 거예요 ('it will go well', 잘되다 'to turn out well' + future -ㄹ 거예요) reassures an anxious person about a FUTURE OUTCOME — a test result, a job application, a surgery, a new relationship. It calms worry about how things will turn out, which is its clear dividing line from 힘내세요 (strength for the present struggle) and 화이팅 (energy for the effort itself). The three smooth stacking: 너무 걱정 마세요 → 잘될 거예요 → 응원할게요. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice: 잘되다 is intransitive 'turn out well', so 잘될 거예요 ≠ 잘할 거예요 ('will perform well' — active doer). Also the spelling: it is 거예요, never 꺼에요 or 거에요. To an elder, add honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요. Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) ↔ 잘될 거예요 (polite) ↔ 잘되실 거예요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 잘되다 = 'to turn out well' (intransitive — things go well by themselves). 잘될 거예요 = 'it will turn out well.' In use, it is the 'don't worry, it'll be fine' reassurance about an outcome the listener is anxious about — not a promise about their performance, but about how things will unfold.

Use it when someone is anxious about a result or outcome: an exam result, a job interview, a medical procedure, starting over. It looks FORWARD to how things will resolve. To a peer or younger person: 잘될 거예요. To an elder: 잘되실 거예요 (with honorific -시-). Banmal to close friends: 잘될 거야.

잘될 거예요 (outcome: 'it'll turn out fine') vs 힘내세요 (strength for the current struggle: 'hang in there') vs 화이팅 (energy pump-up for the effort: 'go for it'). These three layer beautifully: 힘내세요, 화이팅, 잘될 거예요 — covering the present, the push, and the outcome.
Register: 잘될 거야 (banmal) → 잘될 거예요 (polite) → 잘되실 거예요 (honorific). Warmer: 다 잘될 거예요, 분명히 잘될 거예요. Stacks with: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.

Two traps: (1) confusing 잘될 거예요 (things will turn out well — intransitive) with 잘할 거예요 (you/I will perform well — active doer); the verbs are different; (2) misspelling the future as 꺼에요 or 거에요 — the standard written form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.

mistakes: Saying 잘할 거예요 to comfort someone — that means 'will perform well' (active doer); the reassurance about how things turn out is 잘될 거예요 (intransitive).
Spelling the ending 잘될 꺼에요 / 거에요 — the standard future form is 거예요: 잘될 거예요.
Using bare 잘될 거야 to an elder — add the honorific -시-: 잘되실 거예요.

usage: polite -세요, to a peer or someone you respect
the uncontracted form — identical meaning, slightly softer and more careful
reassurance plus a concrete offer — far more comforting than the phrase alone
examples: A: 일이 잘못될까 봐 불안해요 / B: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요.
A: I'm anxious it'll go wrong / B: Don't worry too much — it'll work out.
the bare reassurance; stacking with 잘될 거예요 is the natural complete comfort phrase
시험 걱정하는 동생에게 "너무 걱정 마, 충분히 준비했잖아" 했어요.
To my anxious younger sibling I said, 'Don't worry — you've prepared enough, haven't you?'
everyday: comfort in banmal, grounded with a reminder of their effort
환자 보호자분께 "너무 걱정 마세요. 최선을 다하겠습니다" 하고 안심시켰어요.
To the patient's guardian I said, 'Please don't worry. We will do our very best,' as reassurance.
real situation: professional reassurance, softened with 너무, followed by a commitment — the formula in medical or care settings
nuance: 너무 걱정 마세요 means 'don't worry too much' — 너무 'too (much)' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't.' The 너무 is essential: without it, bare 걱정 마세요 is correct but can sound slightly blunt ('stop worrying'), while 너무 softens it to 'don't worry SO much', acknowledging the concern is understandable. Grammatically, 마세요 is the polite prohibitive of 말다, not 안 + verb; the common English-learner error 안 걱정하세요 is wrong. The dividing line from 잘될 거예요 is direction: 걱정 마세요 addresses the WORRY itself ('ease up on the fretting'), while 잘될 거예요 addresses the OUTCOME ('it'll be fine') — they pair beautifully and almost always appear together. Register: 걱정 마 (banmal) ↔ 걱정 마세요 (polite) ↔ 걱정 마십시오 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 너무 'too much' + 걱정 'worry' + 마세요 'please don't' = 'please don't worry too much.' The 너무 is a softener — it acknowledges the person's concern is understandable, it just asks them not to worry EXCESSIVELY. Without 너무, the phrase is fine but a touch more direct.

Use it when someone is clearly anxious about an outcome, situation, or decision. Polite -세요 works for peers and can be used toward seniors who are worried. Banmal 걱정 마 is warm for friends. In professional settings (medical, legal, service), 걱정 마세요 + a commitment (제가 도와드릴게요 / 최선을 다하겠습니다) is a complete, reassuring phrase.

걱정 마세요 (target: the worry — 'ease up') vs 잘될 거예요 (target: the outcome — 'it'll be fine'). Natural pair: 너무 걱정 마세요, 잘될 거예요. Against 괜찮아요 ('it's okay / don't worry'): 괜찮아요 is shorter and more all-purpose; 걱정 마세요 specifically addresses an anxious person's ongoing worry.
Prohibitive forms: 걱정 마 (banmal) → 걱정 마세요 (polite) → 걱정 마십시오 (formal). Full uncontracted: 걱정하지 마세요. With 너무: 너무 걱정 마세요. Softer still: 너무 걱정하지 않으셔도 돼요.

Two traps: (1) building the prohibition with 안: 안 걱정하세요 is wrong; use 말다 → 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요; (2) using bare 걱정 마 with an elder or in a serious context — 걱정 마세요 is the right polite form, and for real formality, 걱정 마십시오.

mistakes: Forming the negative as 안 걱정하세요 — a prohibition uses 말다: 걱정하지 마세요 / 걱정 마세요, never 안 + verb here.
Saying bare 걱정 마 to an elder or boss — use 걱정 마세요 or 걱정 마십시오.
Confusing 걱정 마세요 (address the worry) with 잘될 거예요 (address the outcome) — natural comfort uses both together.

usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
banmal, to a close friend or child
격식 -습니다, a speech, award ceremony, or formal note
네가 identifies the person you're proud of — natural in banmal
examples: A: 저 전국 1등 했어요! / B: 우와, 정말 자랑스러워요!
A: I came in first in the whole country! / B: Wow, I'm so proud of you!
the bare expression of pride at a remarkable achievement
졸업식 날 딸에게 "우리 딸, 진짜 자랑스러워" 했어요.
On graduation day I told my daughter, 'I'm so proud of you, my girl.'
everyday: a parent's pride in banmal toward a child — the most natural direction for this expression
후배가 큰 상을 받았을 때 "네가 우리 팀의 자랑이야. 정말 자랑스러워" 했어요.
When the junior won a major award I said, 'You're our team's pride. I'm truly proud of you.'
real situation: pairs with 자랑이야 ('you're our pride/glory') for a fuller compliment; senior → junior direction
nuance: 자랑스러워요 ('to feel proud', from 자랑 'pride/boasting' + -스럽다 'to feel like') expresses pride in someone's achievement or in who they are. The DIRECTION rule is crucial and uniquely Korean: pride flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a senior to a junior, or between peers. Telling a teacher, boss, or elder 자랑스러워요 sounds odd and presumptuous, as if you are positioned above them evaluating their worth; toward a respected senior, 존경스러워요 ('I admire/respect you') or 대단하세요 is far more natural. The dividing line: 자랑스럽다 (pride, looking down or across) vs 존경스럽다 (respect, looking up). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this cultural gap — English 'I'm proud of you' is freely said to anyone, including a teacher, so learners aim 자랑스러워요 at their Korean tutor and it lands awkwardly. Note the ㅂ-irregular conjugation: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요. Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) ↔ 자랑스러워요 (polite) ↔ 자랑스럽습니다 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 자랑 means 'something one boasts about with pride.' -스럽다 means 'to feel like, to be full of.' So 자랑스럽다 = 'feels like something to be proud of / makes me feel proud.' In practice, it says 'I'm proud of you' — the speaker's internal feeling of pride at someone else's achievement.

Crucially flows DOWNWARD or sideways — a parent to a child, a teacher to a student, a senior to a junior, or between close peers. Do NOT say it upward to a teacher or boss — it implies you are positioned above them. To an elder you admire, use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

자랑스럽다 (pride, pointing downward/sideways) vs 존경스럽다 (respect/admiration, pointing upward). Confusingly similar: 자랑스럽다 (I feel proud OF someone) vs 자랑하다 (to brag/show off — 자랑하지 마 = 'don't brag', a negative sense of 자랑).
ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스럽다 → 자랑스러워요 (not 자랑스럽어요). Register: 자랑스러워 (banmal) → 자랑스러워요 (polite) → 자랑스럽습니다 (formal). Intensify: 정말/진짜 자랑스러워요, 네가 자랑스러워.

The English-speaker pitfall is the direction rule — English 'I'm proud of you' is used freely toward anyone including a teacher or boss. In Korean, 자랑스러워요 upward at a senior sounds presumptuous ('I'm proud of you' implies you are grading them from above). Say 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요 instead.

mistakes: Saying 자랑스러워요 to a teacher, boss, or elder — pride implies a higher position; toward a senior use 존경스러워요 or 대단하세요.
Conjugating it 자랑스럽어요 — 자랑스럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: 자랑스러워요.
Confusing 자랑스럽다 (proud of someone) with 자랑하다 (to boast/show off) — 자랑하지 마 means 'don't brag', a different sense of 자랑.

english: That looks nice / It's good to see.
usage: it looks nice / good to see
polite -요, to a peer or younger
you look great / it's lovely to see (respectful)
honorific -으시-, noticing tone, to an elder
-네요 adds a warm, observational noticing tone
examples: A: (커플 사진을 보여주며) / B: 와, 두 분 정말 보기 좋아요.
A: (showing a couple photo) / B: Wow, you two really look great together.
the warm approval of a wholesome scene — not just prettiness, but a good-to-witness sight
살 빠진 친구한테 "얼굴도 좋아 보이고 보기 좋다" 했어요.
To my friend who lost weight I said, 'Your face looks well, and you look good.'
everyday: 보기 좋다 approves a healthier, happier appearance — wholesome rather than merely pretty
오랜만에 만난 두 분이 사이좋게 계셔서 "두 분 보기 좋으시네요" 했어요.
Seeing the two of them getting along so warmly, I said, 'It's truly lovely to see you two together.'
real situation: honorific 보기 좋으시네요 toward elders, expressing warm approval of their relationship or wellbeing
nuance: 보기 좋아요 (보다 'to see' + -기 nominalizer + 좋다 'good' = 'good to look at') is the warm 'that looks nice / it's heartwarming to see' you say about a pleasing or wholesome sight — a happy couple, someone glowing with health, people getting along beautifully, a tidy home. It often carries APPROVAL of a wholesome scene rather than just visual prettiness, which is its dividing line from 예뻐요 (purely visual prettiness) and 멋있어요 (cool/impressive): 보기 좋다 = 'this is a beautiful thing to witness.' The English-speaker pitfall is the fixed structure: learners try 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기, but the correct nominalized form is 보기 좋다. Also, 보기 좋아요 ('nice to see') differs from 좋아 보여요 ('looks good / appears to be in good condition') — the word order is reversed and the meaning shifts. Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) ↔ 보기 좋아요 (polite) ↔ 보기 좋으세요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 보기 = 'the act of seeing' (보다 'see' + -기 nominalizer); 좋아요 = 'is good.' Literal: 'the seeing of it is good' = 'it's good to look at.' In use, it is the warm 'looks nice / heartwarming to see' — applies to wholesome scenes, not just visual beauty.

Use it when a scene or person gives you a warm, positive feeling: a happy couple, someone looking healthy, two friends getting along, a nicely arranged space. It is warmer and more approving than just 예뻐요. To an elder, use 보기 좋으시네요. Between friends, bare 보기 좋아 feels natural and genuine.

보기 좋아요 vs 예뻐요: 예뻐요 says the thing itself is pretty; 보기 좋아요 says it is good/wholesome to witness. Against 좋아 보여요: 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good (in condition/health)' — reversed word order, different meaning. Against 멋있어요: 멋있어요 = cool/impressive; 보기 좋아요 = heartwarming/wholesome to see.
Register: 보기 좋아 (banmal) → 보기 좋아요 (polite) → 보기 좋으세요 (honorific). Noticing tone: 보기 좋네요, 보기 좋으시네요. For two people: 두 분 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋아요.

Two traps: (1) restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다, with 보기 (nominalizer) first; (2) confusing it with 좋아 보여요 — the reversed word order shifts the meaning from 'nice to see' to 'looks to be in good condition'; they are related but not interchangeable.

mistakes: Restructuring it as 좋게 보여요 or 좋아 보기 — the fixed expression is 보기 좋다: 보기 좋아요.
Mixing it up with 좋아 보여요 — 보기 좋아요 = 'nice to see', while 좋아 보여요 = 'looks good/well' (condition); related but not identical.
Using bare 보기 좋아 toward an elder you're complimenting — use the honorific 보기 좋으세요 / 보기 좋으시네요.

english: I'm jealous / I envy you (in a good way).
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
exclamatory -다, said with feeling as a burst of admiring envy
examples: A: 저 다음 주에 하와이 가요! / B: 와, 진짜 부러워요!
A: I'm going to Hawaii next week! / B: Wow, I'm so jealous!
the bare good-natured envy as a bright reaction to someone's good news
친구가 새 집 샀다고 해서 "와, 진짜 부럽다" 했어요.
Since my friend bought a new house I said, 'Wow, I'm so jealous.'
everyday: used as a warm compliment dressed as envy — the positive tone is key; it celebrates their good fortune
동안인 선배한테 "피부가 너무 좋으세요. 부러워요" 했어요.
To my youthful-looking senior I said, 'Your skin is amazing. I'm jealous.'
real situation: 부러워요 as a flattering compliment about looks or life circumstances — pairs naturally after a direct observation
nuance: 부러워요 ('I'm envious', from 부럽다 'to be enviable') functions in Korean as a FRIENDLY compliment far more than a complaint — said brightly with a smile, it means 'lucky you / I wish that were me' and warmly congratulates someone's good fortune. The dividing line is against 질투하다 (resentful jealousy that wishes the other person ill) and 샘나다 (petty envy, often between rivals): 부럽다 is the harmless, openly admiring kind, making it a beloved compliment rather than a grievance. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: conjugation (부럽다 is ㅂ-irregular → 부러워요, never 부럽어요), and avoiding it because 'jealous' sounds negative in English — with a bright tone, 부러워요 is a beloved social phrase; flatten the tone, though, and it tips into sounding genuinely resentful. Register: 부러워 (banmal) ↔ 부러워요 (polite) ↔ 부럽습니다 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 부럽다 = 'to be enviable / to make one feel envious.' 부러워요 = 'I find that enviable / I envy you.' In social use, it functions as a warm compliment: 'you're lucky, I want that too' — celebratory, not resentful. Think of it as 'oh, I envy you!' said with a grin.

Use it freely among friends and peers when reacting to good news: a trip, a promotion, a great meal, beautiful skin, a new relationship. Delivery tone is everything: bright = compliment ('lucky you!'), flat = genuine envy or complaint. In formal settings, 부럽습니다 works for politely expressed admiration.

부럽다 (friendly, admiring envy — purely positive) vs 질투하다 (resentful jealousy — implies ill-will toward the other person) vs 샘나다 (petty, slightly childish envy between rivals). When in doubt, 부럽다 is the safe, warm one; 질투 implies a darker emotion.
ㅂ-irregular: 부럽다 → 부러워요 (not 부럽어요). Register: 부러워 (banmal) → 부러워요 (polite) → 부럽습니다 (formal). Intensified: 진짜 부럽다, 너무 부러워요. Combined: 너무 좋겠다, 부러워요.

Two traps: (1) conjugating it 부럽어요 — 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the correct form is 부러워요; (2) avoiding it because 'jealous' sounds negative in English — with a bright tone, 부러워요 is a beloved compliment ('lucky you'); only flat delivery makes it sound genuinely resentful.

mistakes: Conjugating it 부럽어요 — 부럽다 is a ㅂ-irregular: the correct form is 부러워요.
Avoiding it because 'jealous' sounds negative — said with a smile, 부러워요 is a warm compliment ('lucky you'), not a complaint.
Using 질투해요 to mean friendly envy — 질투 is resentful jealousy; the admiring kind is 부러워요.

english: I'll be rooting for you / I've got your back.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
격식 -겠습니다, a formal pledge of support
I'll always be rooting for you
항상 makes it a lasting, ongoing promise — not just for this one event
examples: A: 저 이번에 도전해 보려고요! / B: 응원할게요, 잘할 수 있어요!
A: I'm going to give it a try this time! / B: I'm rooting for you — you can do it!
the bare pledge of personal support, combined with belief in them
시험 앞둔 친구에게 "내가 응원할게, 분명 잘될 거야" 했어요.
To my friend before the exam I said, 'I'm rooting for you — it'll definitely work out.'
everyday: banmal support pledge, paired with reassurance — 응원할게 feels like a personal promise
퇴사하고 창업한다는 선배께 "새로운 도전 진심으로 응원하겠습니다" 하고 인사드렸어요.
To the senior starting a business after leaving I said, 'I sincerely support your new challenge.'
real situation: formal 응원하겠습니다 for a serious life step by a senior — the -겠- signals earnest commitment
nuance: 응원할게요 (應援, 응원 'support/cheering' + -ㄹ게요 'I will, for you') is a personal pledge — 'I'll cheer you on / I'm in your corner' — that promises ongoing backing for someone's effort or challenge. The -ㄹ게요 ending is the key: it is a speaker's promissory 'I commit to this, for your sake', not just a flat prediction, which is the dividing line from 응원할 거예요 ('I will cheer', a neutral future statement). It is also warmer and more committed than 화이팅: 화이팅 is a quick shout in the moment, while 응원할게요 promises you personally will keep backing them over time. The English-speaker pitfall is the spelling: learners write 응원할께요 (wrong — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요, though pronounced tensely as 께). Register: 응원할게 (banmal) ↔ 응원할게요 (polite) ↔ 응원하겠습니다 (formal).

structuredNuance.t: 응원 (應援) = 'support, cheering, backing.' -ㄹ게요 = promissory future: 'I will (for you).' So 응원할게요 = 'I commit to rooting for you.' In use, it is a warm personal pledge — 'I've got your back, I'll keep cheering you on' — more than just saying 'good luck.'

Use it when someone is taking on a challenge, starting something new, or needs sustained encouragement: a job change, a hard exam season, a creative project, a difficult relationship. It implies ongoing support, not just a one-time cheer. To peers and younger people: 응원할게요. To a senior or in formal settings: 응원하겠습니다.

응원할게요 (personal ongoing pledge: 'I'll keep rooting for you') vs 화이팅 (immediate in-the-moment cheer: 'go!'). Against 잘될 거예요 (outcome reassurance: 'it'll work out'): these three layer naturally — 화이팅, 응원할게요, 잘될 거예요 — to cover the push, the backing, and the outcome.
Register: 응원할게 (banmal) → 응원할게요 (polite) → 응원하겠습니다 (formal). Durational: 항상 응원할게요, 끝까지 응원할게요. Intensified: 진심으로 응원할게요.

Two traps: (1) spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요 (written 게, though it sounds tense like 께); (2) substituting 응원할 거예요 — that is a flat prediction ('I will cheer') with no warmth or commitment to the listener; 할게요 carries the personal, promissory weight.

mistakes: Spelling it 응원할께요 — the standard promissory ending is -ㄹ게요: 응원할게요 (pronounced with a tense 께 sound but written 게).
Using 응원할 거예요 instead — that is a flat prediction 'I will cheer'; the warm promise to the listener is 응원할게요.
Treating it as identical to 화이팅 — 화이팅 is an in-the-moment shout, while 응원할게요 pledges ongoing, personal support.

english: It suits you / It looks good on you.
usage: polite -요, to a peer or younger
너무 boosts the compliment — the natural intensifier for this expression
examples: A: (새 안경 쓰고) 어때요? / B: 진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요!
A: (in new glasses) How is it? / B: It really suits you — looks like it was made for you!
the go-to reaction to a new look; 완전 잘 맞는 것 같아요 adds extra warmth
원피스 입은 친구에게 "그 원피스 색깔이 너랑 진짜 잘 어울려" 했어요.
To my friend in a dress I said, 'That dress color really suits you.'
everyday: name the specific item/color + 너랑 잘 어울려 — the natural collocation pattern
머리 자른 부장님께 "새로 하신 머리 스타일 잘 어울리세요" 했어요.
To the manager with a new haircut I said, 'That new hairstyle suits you well, sir.'
real situation: honorific 잘 어울리세요 toward a senior's new look — head straight to this form with anyone older
nuance: 잘 어울려요 (잘 'well' + 어울리다 'to match/go together') is the everyday 'it suits you / it looks good on you' for clothes, glasses, a new haircut, a makeup style, or a color — and the single most natural thing to say when someone shows off a new look. The key dividing line from 예뻐요/멋있어요: 예뻐요 judges the THING itself ('that outfit is pretty'), while 잘 어울려요 says it MATCHES THE PERSON ('that outfit fits you'), which flatters the wearer directly and is why Koreans reach for it constantly as a compliment. The English-speaker pitfall is the grammar: 어울리다 is INTRANSITIVE, so you never attach an object particle; and the natural partner is the particle 랑/이랑/하고 ('goes WITH' the person) — 그 색이 너랑 잘 어울려, not 너를. Also: drop 잘 and bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches', not a compliment. Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) ↔ 잘 어울려요 (polite) ↔ 잘 어울리세요 (honorific).

structuredNuance.t: 잘 = 'well'; 어울리다 = 'to match, go together harmoniously.' 잘 어울려요 literally 'goes together well' — in practice it means 'it suits you / it looks great on you.' The compliment is about the FIT between person and item, not the item in isolation.

Use it when someone tries on or shows off a new outfit, glasses, hairstyle, hair color, or makeup. It is the warmest, most direct compliment on a new look. To peers and younger people: 잘 어울려요. To an elder: 잘 어울리세요. You can also use it for two people who look good together: 두 분 잘 어울리세요.

잘 어울려요 (suits the person — the fit between person and item) vs 예뻐요 (the item itself is pretty, not about the wearer) vs 멋있어요 (it's cool/impressive, not about fit). 어울리다 vs 맞다: 잘 어울려요 is about harmonious matching (style, color); 잘 맞아요 is about physical fit (size).
Register: 잘 어울려 (banmal) → 잘 어울려요 (polite) → 잘 어울리세요 (honorific). Intensified: 너무/진짜 잘 어울려요, 완전 잘 어울려. For two people: 두 사람 잘 어울려요.

Two traps: (1) adding an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing goes WITH you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요; (2) dropping 잘 (bare 어울려요 sounds neutral 'it matches' — the warm compliment keeps 잘 'suits you WELL').

mistakes: Using an object particle (그 옷을 잘 어울려요) — 어울리다 is intransitive; the thing 'goes with' you: 그 옷이 너랑/너한테 잘 어울려요.
Dropping 잘 and saying bare 어울려요 — the compliment keeps 잘 ('suits you well'); without it, it sounds like a flat 'it matches'.
Saying 예뻐요 when you mean it flatters the person — 예뻐요 praises the item itself, while 잘 어울려요 says it suits the wearer.
Using bare 잘 어울려 to an elder — raise it to the honorific 잘 어울리세요 when complimenting a senior's outfit or hair.
